title: A stack machine, proved
objective: Prove that compiling an arithmetic expression to a stack machine preserves its value, by induction on the expression with the stack left arbitrary, and name the hypothesis the plus case needs.

blocks.md: The validator you ran in LAB-9.1 checked one compiled command. A proof checks every program a compiler can produce. Start with the smallest compiler there is: arithmetic over account balances, compiled to a stack machine. Isabelle's HOL-IMP library proves this theorem in a few lines, and the port below reads balances with `bal a`.

choice.prompt: Isabelle proves the stack-machine theorem by induction on the expression, with the stack left arbitrary. Why must the stack be arbitrary?

options.text: The theorem never uses the stack.
options.why: The conclusion mentions `stk`, and the plus case changes it.

options.text: The code for the second operand runs on a stack that already holds the first operand's value.
options.why: Its hypothesis is needed at `aval e₁ s :: stk`, not at `stk`.

options.text: It only makes the automation faster.
options.why: Without it the plus case cannot be proved at all, however much automation runs.

options.text: The induction is on the stack, not on the expression.
options.why: The induction is on the expression. The stack is generalized so the hypothesis covers every stack.

blocks.md:
The machine keeps a stack of integers. `loadi v` pushes a constant, `load a` pushes the balance of account `a`, and `add` pops two values and pushes their sum. The compiler emits the code for the first operand, then the code for the second, then `add`. The theorem: running `comp e` on any stack pushes `aval e s`, the expression's value in store `s`, and leaves the rest of the stack alone.

Two lemmas carry it. `exec_append` says that running two programs back to back is running one and then the other. `exec_comp` is the theorem. `add` on a stack with fewer than two values returns it unchanged, a junk case that compiled code never reaches.

blocks.direction: Replay shows: `exec_comp` one tactic at a time, with the goal after each, then `exec_comp_narrow`, the same induction with `generalizing stk` removed. Compare the stack each hypothesis talks about with the stack the goal needs.

code.text:
abbrev Acct := Nat
abbrev Store := Acct → Int

inductive AExp where
  | n (v : Int)
  | bal (a : Acct)
  | plus (e₁ e₂ : AExp)

def aval : AExp → Store → Int
  | .n v, _ => v
  | .bal a, s => s a
  | .plus e₁ e₂, s => aval e₁ s + aval e₂ s

inductive Instr where
  | loadi (v : Int)
  | load (a : Acct)
  | add

def exec1 (s : Store) : Instr → List Int → List Int
  | .loadi v, stk => v :: stk
  | .load a, stk => s a :: stk
  | .add, j :: i :: stk => (i + j) :: stk
  | .add, stk => stk

def exec (s : Store) : List Instr → List Int → List Int
  | [], stk => stk
  | i :: is, stk => exec s is (exec1 s i stk)

def comp : AExp → List Instr
  | .n v => [.loadi v]
  | .bal a => [.load a]
  | .plus e₁ e₂ => comp e₁ ++ comp e₂ ++ [.add]

theorem exec_append (s : Store) (p q : List Instr) (stk : List Int) :
    exec s (p ++ q) stk = exec s q (exec s p stk) := by
  induction p generalizing stk with
  | nil => rfl
  | cons i is ih => simp [exec, ih]

theorem exec_comp (s : Store) (e : AExp) (stk : List Int) :
    exec s (comp e) stk = aval e s :: stk := by
  induction e generalizing stk with
  | n v => rfl
  | bal a => rfl
  | plus e₁ e₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
    simp only [comp]
    rw [exec_append, exec_append, ih₁, ih₂]
    rfl

-- the same induction with `generalizing stk` left out
theorem exec_comp_narrow (s : Store) (e : AExp) (stk : List Int) :
    exec s (comp e) stk = aval e s :: stk := by
  induction e with
  | n v => rfl
  | bal a => rfl
  | plus e₁ e₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
    simp only [comp]
    rw [exec_append, exec_append, ih₁, ih₂]
    rfl

tap.property: running the compiled code leaves the expression's value on top of the stack

call.prompt: In `exec_comp_narrow`, which case leaves a goal that the hypotheses cannot close?

options.why: A constant pushes one value and needs no hypothesis.
A balance read pushes one value and needs no hypothesis.
The hypothesis for `e₂` speaks about `stk`, but the goal needs it at `aval e₁ s :: stk`.
It is the same slip as SP-2.3's ungeneralized `run_conserves`, and Lean stops the same way.

blocks.after: Lean stops in the `plus` case at `rw [ih₂]` {{run:RUN-lean-stack-machine}}. The first hypothesis applies at `stk`. The second needs the stack that the first operand's code left behind, and a hypothesis tied to one stack cannot supply it. `n` and `bal` close either way.

blocks.md: Read the working `plus` case as four moves in a fixed order: split the code with `exec_append`, use the hypothesis for `e₁` at `stk`, use the hypothesis for `e₂` at `aval e₁ s :: stk`, then compute `add`. `generalizing stk` is what makes each hypothesis a promise about every stack.

choice.prompt: A variant machine adds `minus e₁ e₂`, compiled as `comp e₁ ++ comp e₂ ++ [.sub]`. Lay out its case of `exec_comp` from these blocks. (1) Split the code with `exec_append`, twice. (2) Use `ih₁` at `stk`. (3) Use `ih₂` at `stk`. (4) Use `ih₂` at `aval e₁ s :: stk`. (5) Compute `sub`. (6) Rewrite with the goal itself. Which order is a proof?

options.why: Block 3 applies the hypothesis for `e₂` at `stk`, which is not the stack its code runs on.
Split, run `e₁` on `stk`, run `e₂` on what `e₁` left, then compute `sub`.
Block 4 needs `aval e₁ s :: stk`, which only exists after block 2 has run.
Rewriting with the goal uses the theorem to prove itself.

choice.prompt: A second variant adds `times e₁ e₂`, compiled as `comp e₁ ++ comp e₂ ++ [.mul]`. In its case of `exec_comp`, which instance of the hypothesis for `e₂` is needed?

options.why: That stack is the one before `e₁`'s code has run.
The base case starts empty, but this case starts wherever the whole expression started.
That would be the stack after `e₂`'s own code, so the order is reversed.
The code for `e₂` runs after `e₁`'s value is on the stack.
